bull.b: A consumables-driven model (disposable pods replaced regularly) creates predictable, repeat revenue and high lifetime customer value. This structural cash flow cadence supports durable sales visibility, recurring gross-margin contribution and easier planning for manufacturing and distribution investments.

bull.t: Multi-year revenue scale and high gross margins
bull.b: Sustained rapid revenue growth alongside industry-leading gross margins signals structural competitiveness in product design and manufacturing. High margins provide operating leverage as scale grows, enabling reinvestment in R&D, commercial expansion and margin-resilient profitability over the medium term.

bull.t: Strengthened cash generation and balance sheet
bull.b: A turnaround from negative to multi-hundred-million FCF materially improves financial flexibility. Consistent free cash enables capex for capacity, selective buybacks and debt reduction, reducing leverage risk and giving management choices to support durable growth and withstand execution hiccups.

bear.b: Large-scale corrections and reported serious adverse events impose direct remediation costs and elevate regulatory and reputational risk. Persistent or recurring manufacturing quality issues can erode provider/payer trust, complicate reimbursement, slow new customer adoption and increase ongoing compliance and quality-control expenses.

A growing Type 2 customer segment can exhibit higher early attrition versus Type 1 users, reducing pods-per-patient lifetime. Structural declines in retention lower recurring revenue and weaken unit economics, requiring sustained investment in onboarding, education and care programs to preserve long-term refill volumes.

bear.t: Capex ramp limits near-term free cash flow expansion
bear.b: Planned manufacturing and automation investments are necessary for scale but compress near-term cash conversion. Flat FCF despite rapid revenue growth reduces optionality for accelerated deleveraging or additional shareholder returns, and raises execution risk if capacity investments lag demand or cost more than anticipated.
